item.title: At Karaoke Night, These Exonerated New Yorkers Voice Their Freedom
item.description:
For Jeffrey Deskovic and Alan Newton, normal nights out are no longer just that. They are celebrations of life and expressions of a freedom they didn’t always have.

So when the two men, who were exonerated and released from prison 20 years ago, decided to celebrate their two decades on the outside last Friday evening, where and how they would mark the anniversary was hardly in doubt.

They would eat, drink and dance at Lux Bar and Grill in West Harlem. And there would be karaoke.

The bar is owned by Jabar Walker, who has lived in the neighborhood most of his life, outside of the 25 years he himself spent in prison for a crime he did not commit. And after the bewildering ordeal of decades of wrongful incarceration, he, like some of the men and women thrust back into society, has found karaoke to be something of a re-entry ritual.

Mr. Newton and Mr. Deskovic spent a night at a Union Square karaoke bar upon their releases from prison back in 2006, alongside staff from the Innocence Project, an organization that has worked for more than 30 years to overturn wrongful convictions and push for criminal justice reform. Now, publicly singing their favorite songs remains a friendly and familiar way to gather.

“It was really healing in those first couple of years,” Mr. Deskovic said. “I really was kind of lost socially, but whenever we would have a night, like once every month or sometimes two, I would be in a room full of safe people, people from the Innocence Project, and we would sing.”

And last Friday, sing they did.

The men were among many people crowded into the bar who performed some of their favorite karaoke songs, transporting a space that reopened this summer back to the year 1986. There was the opener, “No Sleep Till Brooklyn” by Beastie Boys, belted out by Mr. Deskovic. Mr. Newton offered a rendition of Earth, Wind & Fire’s “September,” as his 21-year-old nephew, Jamier Parker, sang along by his side. And Mr. Walker performed “Where I Wanna Be,” a classic R&B joint by Donell Jones about reckoning with the fallout of falling out of love.

Mr. Walker was exonerated and released in 2023, after being charged and convicted on two counts of second degree murder. A reinvestigation led by a team of lawyers from the Innocence Project and a special unit of the New York County District Attorney’s office led to his release.

After settling with the state, Mr. Walker purchased the bar. It is six blocks from where he grew up and 10 blocks from the police precinct that investigated him.

At the end of “Where I Wanna Be,” Mr. Walker put a spin on the lyrics, saying to the crowd of more than 60 family members, friends, current and former legal and community advocates: “I want to be here at Lux with all of you.”

The night was part family reunion, part rebirth-day party; it was an evening of celebration through the time-honored tradition of making a joyful noise — or, at times, just noise.

Karaoke, the beloved pastime, is widely popular in New York City, but at Lux’s weekly karaoke nights, the act also holds personal meaning.

Vanessa Potkin, the director of special litigation at the Innocence Project who helped organize last Friday’s party, said karaoke was “the perfect antidote” to prison, a place she described as “a toxin to the human spirit.”

Karaoke nights have been a feature of past Innocence Project conferences. In fact, before it had a larger budget, the group threw karaoke fund-raisers to collect funds for clients’ rent, clothes or bills.

“In the early days, karaoke was definitely a way to deal with the stress of just work and life,” she said. But, after the group held the parties a few times with recently exonerated people like Mr. Newton, “it became such a staple of the Innocence Project and community.”

That community continues to grow. Mr. Newton, 65, has a teenage son whom he calls his “miracle baby” after spending years believing he would never start a family. Mr. Deskovic, 52, has earned a law degree and started his own foundation that seeks to exonerate wrongfully convicted men and women. He spent 16 years in prison for a rape and murder. Both men have spent much of the last 20 years pushing for state and federal criminal justice policy reform in the hopes that theirs will one day be among the last cases of wrongful conviction.

“It’s a miracle that I made it home,” Mr. Newton said, noting that if he had not been exonerated, he would have been released as late as 2034, nearly 50 years after his conviction on charges of rape, robbery and assault. He later added: “I appreciate my time on this earth now. There’s always something in your life that really molds and changes you.”

While incarcerated, music was a window to the rest of the world for Mr. Newton. Listening to the radio, he said, he was subjected to a lot of pop hits from the ’80s and ’90s that he normally would not have listened to. He recalled a lot of Michael McDonald. But for Mr. Deskovic, the most affecting song he remembered is “Live to Tell” by Madonna.

In the pop ballad, he said, he can draw a parallel between its lyrics and his own tale: “I have a tale to tell / Sometimes it gets so hard to hide it well / I was not ready for the fall / Too blind to see the writing on the wall.”

Of the song, Mr. Deskovic said, “You can apply that to the story of being falsely accused, ultimately wrongfully convicted and then ultimately exonerated.” Then he headed back to the bar to perform the track with Rebecca Brown, the Innocence Project’s former policy director who also helped plan the night.

Mr. Walker said that a party like Friday’s, much like a good night of karaoke, had helped him in “trying to move on.”

He pointed to a handful of other men socializing outside the bar, many of whom had also been wrongfully convicted and incarcerated, then exonerated. Not all were close to either of the men being celebrated that night but were attending the party to support two of their own.

“Seeing them smile, seeing us gather, seeing us dance, everybody singing,” he said, almost singing himself as he looked on at the scene in front of him. “It just brings me a sense of freedom that I need.”
